true_leverage.ability: You notice structural gaps in markets and methods before peers name them, then you move into those gaps fast enough to claim pricing power.
true_leverage.why_this_one: Your chart holds Indirect Resource at maximum weight (10) — the month pillar Yi Mao places both stem and branch in the learning-and-pattern-recognition function — so absorbing non-standard information costs you almost nothing while it exhausts peers who lack that drive. But Indirect Resource alone would leave you as a perpetual student. What makes this lever work is the pairing: Companion at equal weight (9) gives you the operational speed to act on what you learned before the window closes. Most people with strong Indirect Resource stay in research mode forever because they lack the execution gear. Most people with strong Companion execute fast but inside crowded lanes because they never researched the unclaimed angle. You have both gears, which means you can complete the full loop — spot the gap, enter it, earn from it — faster than someone who has to borrow the missing half from a partner or a team. The other candidate was your Eating God ability to produce visible output, but Eating God sits at zero in your chart, meaning any output you create will feel costly and slow compared to the research and entry phases. Your edge is not in making things; it is in seeing where to go and getting there first.
true_leverage.evidence: Indirect Resource and Companion are jointly heaviest at 10 and 9. The month pillar Yi Mao places Yi stem (Companion to Jia day master under Yin Wood) and Mao branch (Yin Wood, also Companion) in the prime adult-working-years position, so these two functions dominate your operational identity. The Geng day master is slightly strong with a combined strength score of 2, meaning you are not fragile but you are also not so strong that you can ignore resource flow — you must keep the Indirect Resource input running or you lose the edge. Seven Killings at weight 6 and Direct Wealth at weight 9 together form the external-pressure and tangible-outcome axis, but both require you to have already identified the correct target. If you enter a saturated niche, Seven Killings becomes the grind of competing on the same axis as everyone else, and Direct Wealth becomes the exhaustion of price wars. The leverage comes from using Indirect Resource to pick the target before that saturation occurs.

use_cases.scene: You are considering whether to get certified in a widely recognized skill (project management, data analysis, a popular programming language) because peers are earning well in that space. Instead of enrolling, spend one week scanning the job boards, freelance platforms, and niche forums where people in that field complain about what the certification does not teach. Look for the repeated phrase: 'I have the credential but clients keep asking for X and no course covers it.' That X is your entry point. Learn X from non-standard sources (academic papers, adjacent industries, retired practitioners who wrote obscure blog posts), build a minimal proof-of-capability (a template, a before-and-after case, a ten-minute video walkthrough), and start selling X as a standalone micro-service before any training company packages it into a course. You will have four to eight months where you are the only provider who can deliver X without making the client also pay for the commodity certification they already dismissed as insufficient.
use_cases.exact_action: Pick one skill peers are currently getting certified in. Spend seven days reading complaints and gap-reports in forums, Slack groups, Reddit threads, and LinkedIn posts from people who completed that certification. Write down every capability gap mentioned more than three times. Choose the one gap you can close fastest with knowledge you already have or can acquire in two weeks. Build the smallest sellable proof of that capability (a checklist, a script, a one-page audit tool, a recorded walkthrough). Post it for sale or send it to five potential clients as a paid pilot offer. Do not wait to see if a competitor notices the same gap — your edge is in being first, not in being the only one who could have thought of it.
use_cases.why_it_works: Indirect Resource at 10 means you can process scattered, low-status information sources (old blog posts, niche academic papers, complaint threads) faster than peers who only read the official curriculum, and Companion at 9 means you can package and ship a minimal service in days rather than months. The gap between your research speed and your shipping speed is where the profit concentrates. If you delay shipping to make the offer perfect, peers will close the gap and you lose the first-mover pricing power.

use_cases.scene: You are in a salaried role where your job description is stable but you notice that internal requests keep surfacing for a capability the team does not have. Examples: everyone struggles with a legacy system and keeps asking for workarounds; clients keep requesting a feature the product does not support; the finance team manually reconciles data that could be automated but no one has time to build the tool. Do not volunteer to take on this work as an unpaid internal project, and do not wait for management to allocate budget. Instead, treat it as market research. Use your off-hours to build the solution as a reusable external service (a script, a template, a connector, a micro-SaaS tool), then sell it to other companies facing the same problem. Your employer revealed the gap; you supply it to the market while they are still debating whether to prioritize it internally.
use_cases.exact_action: Identify one recurring internal request that your current employer has not solved after three months of complaints. Spend two weeks building a minimal external version of the solution that does not use any proprietary company data or code. Package it as a paid offering (a script on Gumroad, a Zapier template, a Notion database, a consultation hour where you walk someone through the setup). Market it in communities where others face the same problem (industry Slack groups, Reddit, niche LinkedIn posts). Do not tell your employer you are doing this unless your contract forbids external income. The goal is to convert an internal capability gap into external revenue while your employer is still waiting for budget approval. If the employer later wants to buy your solution, you can negotiate terms as an external vendor rather than as an employee doing free extra work.
use_cases.why_it_works: Your Direct Wealth at 9 and Seven Killings at 6 together mean you perform best when there is a clear external demand and a visible competitive frame, but you burn out fast when the work is internal and unpaid because there is no score to validate the effort. Building the external version lets you channel the same capability into the earn leg of the loop, and because you spotted the gap in a contained environment (your employer), you know the demand is real before you build. Indirect Resource at 10 means you can extract the reusable pattern from the specific internal case faster than someone who only sees their employer's unique problem and assumes no one else has it.

use_cases.scene: You are deciding whether to join a startup, take a freelance project, or commit to a new niche. The opportunity looks appealing because the company or client has traction and the work matches your skills. Before you accept, run this test: search LinkedIn, Twitter, and niche job boards for how many other people are already offering the same capability in the same format to the same market. If you find more than twenty providers in the first two pages of results, the niche is saturated and your leverage collapses. You will spend the next year competing on price, brand, or tenure — all factors you cannot change quickly. Walk away and spend that year in a different niche where you can be in the first ten providers. The cut-off is not arbitrary: once a niche has twenty visible providers, clients start filtering by credibility signals you do not yet have (case studies, testimonials, years in business), and your research advantage becomes irrelevant because everyone is working from the same playbook.
use_cases.exact_action: Before accepting any new project, client, or niche commitment, spend one hour searching for existing providers. Use LinkedIn (search job titles and service descriptions), Twitter (search bio keywords and pinned tweets), Google (search 'hire [your service] for [your niche]'), and any niche directories or Slack groups where your target clients gather. Count how many providers appear in the first two pages of results. If the count exceeds twenty, decline the opportunity and spend the same week researching an adjacent niche with fewer than ten visible providers. Do not assume you can out-compete the twenty through better marketing or harder work — your chart has no Eating God or Direct Officer to sustain long visibility campaigns or hierarchical credibility-building. Your edge is in early entry, not in sustained competition.
use_cases.why_it_works: Companion at 9 gives you execution speed, but it does not give you endurance in head-to-head competition. Seven Killings at 6 means you can handle pressure, but only when you are moving toward a clear target, not when you are stuck in a pricing war with peers who entered the niche years before you. Indirect Resource at 10 is your only renewable advantage, but it only renews if you keep moving into new knowledge domains. If you stay in a saturated niche, you stop learning (because everyone already knows the same things) and you lose the lever. The twenty-provider rule is a forcing function: it keeps you in the early-move zone where your research speed still matters.

next_90_days.single_focus: Identify one undersupplied capability niche, build the smallest paid proof-of-concept, and send it to ten potential buyers before the 90-day mark. The niche must meet two criteria: fewer than ten visible providers when you search for it, and you can deliver a working version of the capability within two weeks using knowledge you already have or can acquire in that time. Do not build the perfect version. Do not wait for validation. Do not research how others are pricing it. Your goal is to test whether anyone will pay for this thing while the niche is still unclaimed. If no one responds, you spent two weeks and learned the niche was a mirage. If even two people respond, you have six months of runway to refine the offer before peers notice and enter.
next_90_days.completion_signal: You have sent ten personalized outreach messages (email, LinkedIn DM, Slack DM, or direct pitch in a relevant forum) offering a paid version of the capability, and at least one recipient has either paid you, booked a call to discuss terms, or referred you to someone who needs it. The completion condition is not 'ten people said yes' — it is 'ten people received a concrete offer and you have documented evidence (screenshots, email threads, payment receipts) that you made the offer and at least one person took the next step.' If all ten ignore you, you still completed the action, but you now know this niche does not convert and you move to the next candidate. The falsifiable outcome is: did you actually offer something for money, or did you spend 90 days researching and planning without shipping?
next_90_days.why_90_days: Your Companion at 9 means you can execute a two-week build cycle comfortably, and Indirect Resource at 10 means you can research a new niche in one week if you commit to non-standard sources and skip the bestseller lists. Ninety days gives you time to test three niches if the first two do not convert, but it is short enough that you cannot hide in research mode. The forcing function is the ten outreach messages: you cannot send them unless you built something, and you cannot learn whether the niche is real unless you actually offered it for money. If you reach day 90 and you have not sent ten messages, the analysis is not wrong — you chose not to use the lever, which is itself a data point.

falsification_signals.signal: You complete three different 90-day cycles following this manual, and in all three cycles you send at least ten paid offers into undersupplied niches, and in all three cycles zero people respond, pay, or refer. Not 'people said they would think about it' — zero commercial traction of any kind. If this happens, the analysis is missing something structural about how you convert knowledge into income, and you should stop following this manual. The chart says you can research and move fast, but it does not guarantee that what you research has market demand or that your offer format is intelligible to buyers. Three consecutive failed cycles means either you are picking niches with no real demand, or your offer communication is broken, or the commercial environment you are operating in does not reward early-move research (for example, you are in a credentialing-heavy industry where buyers only hire people with ten years of documented experience, and no amount of niche research bypasses that filter).
falsification_signals.what_to_do_instead: If this signal triggers, spend one month doing the opposite: pick a crowded niche where at least fifty providers are visibly earning, study how the top ten providers structure their offers and pricing, then copy their format exactly and compete on execution speed and reliability rather than on unique positioning. This tests whether your chart can earn in a commodity market when you are not trying to differentiate. If you earn in the commodity test but failed in the niche test, the problem is not your capability — it is that you are overestimating your ability to identify real demand in early markets. Stick to proven niches and use your Companion speed to deliver faster than slower peers, rather than trying to use Indirect Resource to discover new niches.

falsification_signals.signal: You follow this manual and you do generate traction — people pay you, refer you, and ask for more — but after six months you feel more drained than you did in your previous salaried role, you resent client requests, and you start missing deadlines or avoiding the work. If this happens, the analysis correctly identified your lever but you are operating in an environment that penalizes the way you use it. The most common cause: you entered a niche where clients expect high-touch communication, frequent revisions, or ongoing relationship management, and your chart has no Direct Resource or Eating God to sustain that service mode. You can win clients with research and speed, but you cannot retain them if retention requires constant visibility and nurturing.
falsification_signals.what_to_do_instead: If this signal triggers, audit your client mix and identify which clients required the most communication, revisions, or emotional labor per dollar earned. Fire or do not renew those clients, even if they pay well, and focus only on clients who pay for a defined deliverable (a one-time audit, a template, a script, a recorded training) with minimal follow-up. Restructure your offers so that you sell knowledge products (courses, templates, databases, tools) rather than ongoing services (consulting retainers, done-for-you management, client success roles). Your chart can earn from research and fast execution, but it cannot sustain long service relationships without burning out. If you cannot restructure the offers, return to a salaried role where someone else handles client relationships and you only handle the research and delivery legs.
